lead: A beam resists bending; a shaft resists twisting. Bending depends on the second moment about an axis, which you met in 4.4. Twisting depends on the second moment about a point — the polar moment of inertia J. Take every element of area, multiply by the square of its distance from a chosen point, and add. That single number decides how stiff a circular shaft is in torsion. The radius of gyration turns the same number into a distance you can picture: the size of a thin ring that would behave the same way.
prereq: You need: 4.4 for second moments and 4.5 for the perpendicular axis theorem.

sections.h3: The second moment about a point

blocks.text: Pick a point O in the plane of a flat area A. Take a small element of area dA at a straight-line distance r from O. The polar moment of inertia about O adds r² dA over the whole area:

blocks.where: J is the polar moment of area about O, in mm⁴; r is the distance from O to the element dA, in mm; dA is the element area, in mm². The name polar is old: r is measured from a pole (a point), not from an axis line.

blocks.text: Draw x and y axes through O. For any point, r² = x² + y². So J = ∫(x² + y²)dA = ∫x²dA + ∫y²dA = Ix + Iy. Here Ix and Iy are the second moments about the x and y axes, both passing through the same point O, in mm⁴. This is the perpendicular axis theorem of 4.5, read as a definition: the polar moment about a point equals the sum of two rectangular moments about any two perpendicular axes through that point.

The condition is a flat area and the same point. If O is the centroid, J is the centroidal polar moment. If O is any other point, Ix and Iy must both be taken about axes through that other point, not about the centroidal axes. Adding a centroidal Ix to a non-centroidal Iy is the commonest error in this chapter.

For a solid circle of diameter d, take a ring of radius r and width dr. Its area is dA = 2πr dr. Then J = ∫ from 0 to d/2 of r²(2πr dr) = 2π[r⁴/4] = πd⁴/32. For a hollow circle with outside diameter D and inside diameter d, subtract the hole: J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32.

head: Shape
Polar second moment about the centroid
rows: Hollow circle, outside D, inside d

blocks.text: By symmetry a circle has Ix = Iy about any pair of perpendicular diameters. Since J = Ix + Iy, each diameter gives I = J/2 = πd⁴/64. That is the value you already use for a circular beam in bending.

A circular shaft under torque twists by an amount that carries J in the denominator: a larger J means a stiffer shaft. The full torsion formula belongs to a strength of materials course. Here the point is that J is the property of the cross-section that resists twist.

The radius of gyration is the distance at which the whole area could be concentrated, as a thin ring or line, and give the same second moment. Define k = √(I/A) and kₚ = √(J/A). Then I = A k² and J = A kₚ². Here k and kₚ are lengths in mm, I and J are in mm⁴, and A is in mm². k is the radius of gyration about an axis; kₚ is the polar radius of gyration about a point.

For a rectangle b × h, about the centroidal axis parallel to b: I = bh³/12 and A = bh, so k = √(h²/12) = h/√12 = 0.2887h. About the base the same rectangle gives k = h/√3, larger because the area is further from the base.

For a solid circle of diameter d about a diameter, k = √(I/A) = √((πd⁴/64)/(πd²/4)) = √(d²/16) = d/4. About the centre, kₚ = √(J/A) = √((πd⁴/32)/(πd²/4)) = √(d²/8) = d/√8 = 0.3536d. A hollow circle has larger radii of gyration for the same outside diameter, because its area sits further out.

figure.caption: The flow from a point O to the integrals: r is measured from O, the polar moment splits into Ix + Iy for a flat area, and the radii of gyration turn both second moments into distances.

spec.title: From polar moment to radius of gyration
spec.aria: A flow builds the polar moment as the integral of r squared dA, splits it into Ix plus Iy, and defines the radius of gyration from it.

examples.question: A solid steel shaft has diameter 60 mm. Find its cross-sectional area, the polar moment of area about the centre, the second moment about a diameter, and both radii of gyration.
steps: Radius r = d/2 = 30 mm. Area A = πr² = π(30)² = 2827.4 mm².
Second moment about a diameter I = J/2 = 636,172.5 mm⁴. This also equals πd⁴/64.
Radius of gyration k = √(I/A) = √(636,172.5 / 2827.4) = √225.0 = 15.0 mm. This is d/4.
Polar radius of gyration kₚ = √(J/A) = √(1,272,345 / 2827.4) = √450.0 = 21.2 mm. This is d/√8.
examples.check:
import math
d = 60.0
r = d / 2
A = math.pi * r * r
J = math.pi * d**4 / 32
I = J / 2
k = math.sqrt(I / A)
kp = math.sqrt(J / A)
print(round(A, 1))
print(round(J, 1))
print(round(I, 1))
print(round(k, 1))
print(round(kp, 1))

traps: Adding Ix about the centroid to Iy about some other point. Both axes must pass through the same point O, or use the parallel axis theorem first.
Using radius where diameter belongs. J = πd⁴/32 uses diameter; with radius r, J = πr⁴/2.
Quoting k = d/4 for a circle about its centre. About a diameter k = d/4; about the centre kₚ = d/√8.
Forgetting that J = Ix + Iy needs a flat area. For a solid body, the mass moment of inertia about an axis is a different quantity, covered in 4.8.
Mixing units: d in mm gives J in mm⁴, not mm³. The fourth power of a length is an area times an area.

quiz.q: Define the polar moment of inertia of a flat area about a point O.
quiz.a: J = ∫ r² dA, where r is the distance from O to the element dA and dA is the element area. J is in mm⁴.

quiz.q: Write J for a solid circle of diameter d and for a hollow circle of outside D and inside d.
quiz.a: Solid: J = πd⁴/32. Hollow: J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32.

quiz.q: Why does J equal Ix + Iy for a flat area?
quiz.a: For axes through the same point, r² = x² + y² for every element. Integrating r² dA gives ∫x²dA + ∫y²dA, which is Ix + Iy.

quiz.q: What does the radius of gyration tell you physically?
quiz.a: It is the distance at which the whole area could be placed as a thin ring or line and give the same second moment. It measures how far the area is spread from the axis or point.

quiz.q: A hollow shaft has outside diameter 80 mm and inside diameter 60 mm. Find its polar moment of area about the centre.
A rectangle is 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep. Find its polar moment about the centroid and its polar radius of gyration.
The diameter of a solid circular shaft is doubled. What happens to J and to k about a diameter?
quiz.a: J depends on d⁴, so it becomes 2⁴ = 16 times larger. k = d/4, so it doubles. A larger shaft is far stiffer in twist, but its material is used less efficiently than a hollow shaft of the same area.

beyond: Not for the exam. Shafts that are not circular twist with warping, and the cross-section property is then a torsion constant Jₜ that is not πd⁴/32; search 'torsion constant of non-circular section'. Finite element programs store J for each beam element. Flywheel designers use the mass radius of gyration to size a rim. Search 'warping constant' and 'polar moment of inertia shaft design'.
